nameStory: The Canada plum gets its name from its northern range, extending well into Canada where it thrives in cooler climates. It's also called the black plum because its bark often appears quite dark, especially on older trees. The scientific name 'nigra' means black in Latin, referring to this distinctive dark bark coloration.
description: Canada plum is a small native tree or large shrub that typically grows 15-25 feet tall with a rounded, spreading crown. It belongs to the rose family, sharing relatives with apples, cherries, and roses. In spring, it transforms into a cloud of white flowers before the leaves fully emerge, followed by small reddish-purple plums in late summer. The dark, often nearly black bark gives this tree its distinctive appearance year-round.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Dark gray to nearly black bark that feels rough and scaly, often with horizontal lines called lenticels. On younger branches, the bark may have a reddish-brown tinge but darkens with age.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white flowers with 5 rounded petals appear in small clusters of 2-4 blooms in early spring before leaves emerge. Each flower is about an inch across with a sweet, light fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with pointed tips and finely toothed edges, arranged alternately on branches. They feel slightly rough on top and have a matte finish, turning yellow to orange in fall.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Round plums about an inch across, starting green and ripening to red or purple with a waxy bloom. They taste quite sour and astringent when raw, with a large pit inside.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Often grows with multiple trunks or suckers from the base, creating small thickets. Branches tend to spread horizontally, giving the tree a broad, rounded appearance.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Small, pointed brown buds that are pressed close to the twigs. Winter buds are about 1/4 inch long and have several overlapping scales.

habitat: Canada plum grows in forest edges, stream banks, and woodland openings throughout New England, preferring moist but well-drained soils. It's often found in partially sunny spots where forests meet fields or along hiking trails. This adaptable native can handle both acidic and slightly alkaline soils and is cold-hardy enough to thrive even in northern Vermont and New Hampshire.

seasonality.spring: White flowers bloom in early May before leaves fully emerge, creating a striking display. New leaves unfold as bright green and soft to the touch, with visible veining.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage provides dense shade, and small green fruits begin developing. The dark bark becomes more prominent against the green leaves.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to orange-red, and fruits ripen to deep red or purple. This is the best time to spot the edible plums, though they're quite tart.
seasonality.winter: Distinctive dark bark and branching pattern make identification possible. Small buds and occasional persistent fruits help distinguish it from other trees.

funFact: Canada plum fruits were so important to Indigenous peoples that they would burn prairie areas specifically to encourage plum thickets to spread, creating managed 'plum orchards' that could feed entire communities during late summer harvests.
confusionNotes: Canada plum is most easily confused with American plum, but Canada plum has much darker, nearly black bark while American plum bark stays grayish-brown. Memory trick: 'Canada plum wears a black coat for those cold northern winters!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'plum,' Canada plum fruits are quite different from grocery store plums - they're much smaller, more sour, and were traditionally used for jams and jellies rather than eaten fresh. Many people don't realize this native tree produces edible fruit at all.
compareHints: Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries. While beach plum also produces small fruits, it stays much shorter and grows only in coastal areas. Canada plum's flowers appear in small clusters unlike the long drooping clusters of chokecherry or black cherry.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
